findings.title: Generated contract describes mostly happy paths, not the actual HTTP boundary
findings.authority: API-02 requires the generated client to match the server; RFC-001 HTTP contracts require stable machine-readable errors and a complete OpenAPI surface. Rust-derived metadata is the selected local authority, rather than an independently handwritten specification.
evidence: Parsed the complete openapi.json and compared operations to Rust handlers and middleware. GET /v1/auth/sessions declares only 200, but memberships::sessions returns Unauthenticated before calling the application when the session cookie is absent; ApiError serializes that as HTTP 401 with {code: unauthenticated}.

POST /v1/organizations declares only 201 although the shared security middleware returns 403 with an ErrorBody before handler invocation for absent or invalid Origin/CSRF. Other handlers similarly omit ordinary authentication, authorization, input, availability and limit responses. There is no shared default ErrorBody response.

The three confirmation-page operations describe 200 with no response content. Their implementations return Html, while the generated SDK declares content?: never. The installed openapi-fetch implementation defaults parseAs to json at src/index.js:52 and parses successful bodies as JSON at lines 249-262. The SDK adds no HTML-specific handling. A default typed GET to a confirmation route therefore attempts to parse <!doctype html> as JSON rather than delivering the documented result.

The contract has no cookie security scheme or operation security requirements and no Origin/CSRF contract parameters. Request role/action values and role responses are unrestricted strings despite a closed accepted vocabulary. These are additional manifestations of incomplete metadata, not separate runtime authorization-bypass claims.

sdk/tests/client.integration.test.ts obtains the confirmation page using raw fetch rather than the generated client, checks successful paths, and does not exercise typed error access. Drift checks can therefore remain green while faithfully regenerating the wrong contract.
findings.demonstrated_consequence: The public machine-readable contract excludes normal responses. SDK consumers cannot accurately type normal failure branches for success-only operations, and default SDK confirmation-page requests use the wrong body parser. Human readers also cannot discover the required session/CSRF protocol from OpenAPI alone.
findings.remedy: Repair utoipa metadata at the Rust source: share reusable error-response declarations or a justified default error response, declare text/html string bodies, describe cookie authentication and unsafe-request headers, and represent closed transport vocabularies with explicit schema enums. Regenerate OpenAPI and declarations, never edit generated files. Document or wrap parseAs: text for HTML endpoints. Add a small executable contract-conformance matrix instead of relying only on generation drift and a happy-path client journey.
executable_verification: Add HTTP regressions for GET /v1/auth/sessions without a cookie => 401 JSON and POST /v1/organizations without Origin/CSRF => 403 JSON; validate both returned responses against the generated contract.
Add a Bun SDK test that fetches each confirmation page through the intended supported client call and observes text/html without a JSON parse exception.
Add a TypeScript fixture that reads error.code for unauthenticated session listing and forbidden organization creation without casts; run bun node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc --noEmit from sdk.
Run the normal OpenAPI/SDK regeneration and drift gate after the source metadata changes.
findings.verification_status: Source and generated-artifact mismatch established by inspection and complete JSON parsing. Runtime probe prepared but not executed because the compiler invocation was held for approval; do not label this runtime-reproduced.

findings.title: Opening another confirmation tab invalidates the first tab's embedded CSRF token
findings.authority: AUTH-01 and API-03 require a working browser confirmation journey with CSRF protection; safety does not require breaking independent same-origin confirmation pages.
evidence: Each GET of login confirmation or invitation confirmation unconditionally generates and sets a fresh shared Path=/ csrf cookie.
The returned script captures that specific issuance value inside its x-csrf-token header string instead of reading the current cookie at submission.

Security requires exact equality of the submitted header and the current csrf cookie. Tab A receives token A; loading either confirmation page in tab B replaces the shared cookie with token B; tab A still submits header A and is deterministically rejected with 403 before its operation can run.

The scripts clear the fragment using history.replaceState immediately on load. Refreshing tab A to acquire a fresh embedded CSRF value also loses the login or invitation token unless the user reopens the original email link.
The browser suite uses only one page. Its generic mutation helper already reads the current csrf cookie at submission, but the product's actual confirmation buttons do not.
findings.demonstrated_consequence: Ordinary multi-tab use, including signing in in another tab before accepting an invitation, makes a still-valid confirmation link fail. Login reports 'Link invalid or expired' for this unrelated recoverable CSRF mismatch.
findings.remedy: Read the current same-origin csrf cookie when the user clicks, as the SDK/browser helper already does, rather than binding each page to a cookie value that another page can replace. Keep exact-Origin, duplicate-cookie rejection, and explicit user confirmation. Alternatively reuse a valid existing CSRF cookie when rendering, but account for concurrent first loads; do not weaken the server comparison.
executable_verification: Extend sdk/browser.mjs with two pages sharing one BrowserContext: load a valid invitation or login link in A; load /v1/auth/confirmation in B; click A; expect its intended success rather than 403.

Include the actual invitation sequence: open invitation in A, obtain/sign in with the invited email in B, return to A and accept. Assert membership publication and that missing/incorrect CSRF and cross-origin requests remain forbidden.
Retain a valid-token control before opening the second page so expiry or invalid fixture data cannot explain a failure.
findings.verification_status: Deterministic source-level state transition. No browser or live-server reproduction was run in this review.

findings.title: Entrypoints discard all startup failure context, making deployment failures indistinguishable
findings.authority: ARC-02 specifies an error taxonomy and typed configuration; OPS-03 requires useful structured, redacted operational logs. Sanitization is mandatory, but losing even a safe operation/category is not.
evidence: Every executable converts the entire bootstrap Result to is_err() and prints the same startup_or_runtime_failure object, discarding the error before classification.

Config::load propagates missing/invalid configuration, pool creation propagates connection failures, enforce_runtime_role propagates a safety rejection, and listener binding propagates address conflicts. None of those call sites emits a safe failure stage.
The CLI constructs a useful usage error for unknown commands, but main discards it too. Even invoking the CLI incorrectly produces only the same generic runtime message.

The JSON tracing subscriber does not repair this: these early paths return with ? and do not emit classified events. Infrastructure query-category logging covers other adapter failures, not all bootstrap stages.
findings.demonstrated_consequence: Operators cannot distinguish missing configuration, unsafe database credentials, unreachable PostgreSQL, an occupied listener, or invalid command usage from the application's own output. This obstructs the advertised fresh-checkout/deployment workflow and failure diagnosis without improving secrecy beyond what a closed category would provide.
findings.remedy: Preserve a small typed bootstrap error stage/category and emit it once at the executable boundary. Include only safe names such as configuration, database_connect, runtime_role, listener_bind, worker_start and invalid_command; do not log raw DSNs, SMTP credentials, database messages or arbitrary error Display/Debug. Print fixed CLI usage for invalid commands. Avoid a generic error framework or duplicate log-and-rethrow layers.
executable_verification: Add subprocess tests invoking the built CLI with an unknown command and the server with PUBLIC_ORIGIN or DATABASE_URL absent; assert nonzero exit and distinct closed categories or fixed usage.
Add an occupied-loopback-port startup test with disposable dependency configuration; assert listener_bind is distinguishable from dependency failure.
Inject secret-bearing configuration strings and assert neither stderr nor JSON fields disclose them.
findings.verification_status: Direct source-level information-loss proof; no subprocess failure probe run.

clean_path_meaning: No independent actionable defect found in these files. Existing test cases are sound but do not establish the missing scenarios described in the findings. This is not a passing-runtime-gate assertion.
structural_assessment: The API handlers are direct transport adapters: UUID-to-domain-ID conversion, actor lookup, one application operation, explicit response mapping. No SQL or authorization-policy implementation was found in assigned handlers. Organization and membership policy remains application-owned; bootstrap owns construction.

api/src/lib.rs mixes state, errors, middleware, authentication, organizations, projects and contract assembly. A future cohesive split into security/errors and resource modules would improve change locality, but at 570 lines this is not independently treated as a correctness blocker or a size-only finding. Avoid adding controller/service wrappers that merely forward these already-direct calls.

The security middleware combines admission, request deadline, error-envelope normalization and observations. Its route-string allowlist is a maintenance coupling; attach admission to the authentication route group if new auth endpoints are introduced. No currently missing listed authentication admission route was demonstrated.

Cookie parsing preserves duplicate-name ambiguity and rejects parse errors. Cookie construction is library-owned and retains Secure/HttpOnly/session scope. CSRF remains a deliberately documented narrow exact-Origin/double-submit implementation; ADR 002 contains actual library qualification evidence, so this review does not re-demand an incompatible session stack.

Transport layers correctly replace client request IDs outside tracing, record matched templates instead of raw credential-bearing URIs, and apply overriding static headers. Instance-owned Prometheus handles and fresh scrape registries avoid mutable global registries.

SDK wrapper is small and delegates HTTP behavior to openapi-fetch. Its compatibility bundler is a documented compiler-API workaround, not a reason to hand-maintain generated declarations. Lockfile/package versions were inspected together; no package replacement is recommended.

Bootstrap constructs SmtpMailer twice for login and reauthentication even though one immutable Arc can implement both ports. Sharing it would delete duplicate environment reads and transport construction; this is an optional local simplification, not a separate blocker.

Server shutdown stops serving via Axum graceful shutdown and closes the pool afterward; worker termination is propagated from River run.wait. API handler timeouts cancel the handler future, while source admission precedes that timeout by explicit ADR choice. Bootstrap has no outer bounded drain deadline; no production-composed hang was established, so this remains a lifecycle verification gap rather than a claimed reproduced defect.
